assessment: The paper reports no clear change in headache. The linked dysmenorrhea study used both sage and lemon balm and enrolled people without Parkinson disease.
Insomnia appears in the introduction. The pre-post outcome table reports menopausal symptoms including night sweats and fatigue and gives no separate insomnia estimate.
The uncontrolled menopause comparison reports a decrease on the fatigue item during sage extract treatment. It gives no estimate for fresh sage in Parkinson disease.
Melissa officinalis appears in a cited primary dysmenorrhea study. The menopausal study used sage only.
Cherry flavor was in the common placebo base. The randomized arms did not vary consumption of cherries.
The authors cite a prior grape juice study. The trial’s beverages contained apple, blueberry or coffee berry extracts, with no grape arm.
A mixture containing whole coffee fruit extract lowered acute mental fatigue ratings in healthy adults. It supplies no brewed-coffee comparison.
Green tea appears in a cited pharmacokinetic review and caffeine appears in the coffee berry discussion. The trial administered no green tea.
The discussion compares apple polyphenols with evidence on cocoa flavanols. The trial administered no cocoa or dark chocolate.
Sage extract was common to three active mixtures. Two had lower task fatigue in healthy volunteers. The design gives no sage-only contrast.
The healthy-athlete crossover reports lower cycling exertion with a mixture of sage leaf extract and Spanish sage essential oil. It does not estimate clinical fatigue severity.
